Board cards use the catalog's four a2e01 concept ids (llm-apis, messages, roles, system-prompts); strings reach back to tokens (a1e03), context-windows (a1e05), sampling (a1e06), instruction-tuning (a1e07) and statelessness (a1e09), and ahead to prompting (a2e02), tool-calling (a2e05), keys (a6e01), retries (a6e02) and rate-limits (a6e07). title: First Contact
setting: a radio operator calling a station that answers too fast

post.author: u/repeater_hut_teun
post.title: I run the night radio for twelve fire towers, and the station I built answers before I lift my hands. Last night it called the new warden by last week's name, then stopped mid-sentence.

blocks.text: I'm a junior developer, and in lightning season I work nights as the radio operator at Kettlewood Base. Twelve fire towers stand on the ridges around us, each with one warden awake until dawn, watching for strikes. They call me on the radio, and when they ask something I can't answer, I ask the far station.

That's what the wardens call my relay page, a web page on the base laptop. It sends their question to a language model through a provider's API as an HTTP request, the web's way for one program to ask another for something, and reads the answer out on air. Each request carries my API key, the secret that tells the provider which account is calling, the standing orders I wrote, sent as the system prompt, and the tower's conversation so far, which the page saves so follow-up questions work. I set max_tokens, the most the model may write, to 40, so it can't ramble on air. It answers before I've lifted my hands off the keyboard.
At 01:47 last night Marisol, on her first night in Tower 6, asked how to log a strike she couldn't place.

01:47:12  tower 6   Far station, Tower 6, first night on this tower.
                    How do I log a lightning strike I cannot place?
01:47:13  station   Tower 6, far station. Log the time and your best
                    bearing, and count the seconds to the thunder. And
                    Halvard, nobody is on your stairs. It is the tower
                    cooling. Stay in the
Halvard had Tower 6 last week. Marisol hadn't said a word about stairs.

She came back on the radio: Base, who is Halvard? Then, quieter: Base, there's someone on my stairs. At the 02:00 roll call, when my page sends one call for each tower at once, ten of my twelve towers heard station busy. I thought the provider was down.

At three I opened the provider's usage page, which lists every call on my account and what it cost. The net was quiet. My API key wasn't. Since eleven it had made ten calls at the top of every minute, and none of them were mine. Someone else is on my call sign.

The provider's console has a button that revokes an API key, switching it off for good. I haven't pressed it: the net opens again at nine tonight, and my page needs that key. What happened, and what do I change?

diagram.aria: Teun's drawing of the request his page sent at 01:47 and what came back. Top row, three things that went in: the API key, kept in the page's code and sent as the x-api-key header; the system prompt, his standing orders, 42 tokens; Halvard's four turns from last Tuesday, eight messages, 190 tokens, saved and never cleared. Bottom row: Marisol's question, 23 tokens, goes in as the last message; the request, 255 tokens in, max_tokens 40, temperature 0.3; the answer at 01:47:13, stop_reason max_tokens, 40 tokens out.

blocks.caption: Drawn at four this morning from the request my page saved at 01:47. The standing orders went in as the system prompt, 42 tokens. Halvard's four turns from last Tuesday went in as eight messages, 190 tokens, and Marisol's question last, 23. That's 255 tokens in, with max_tokens 40 and temperature 0.3. The answer stopped at 40 tokens, mid-sentence.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in Tower 6 is haunted, and the far station isn't far: it's a language model answering whatever your page sends it, and it keeps nothing between calls, as in case 9. Two names for what's in each request and response. Every message in the conversation carries a role: user for whoever asks, assistant for the model's answers, and the model reads the list in order as one conversation. And every answer comes back with a stop reason, the provider's note of why the model stopped writing. Two questions. Open the request your page sent at 01:47: how many messages were in it, and whose words were they? And on the usage page, how many of last night's calls were yours?

replies.author: u/repeater_hut_teun
replies.text: Nine messages. My page saves each tower's conversation and never clears it, so it sent Halvard's four turns from last Tuesday, user and assistant in turn, eight messages, then Marisol's question as the ninth. 255 tokens in. The response says stop_reason: max_tokens, and its usage says output_tokens: 40. On the usage page, 61 of last night's calls were ours. The other 3,600 came between eleven and five, ten at the top of every minute: 7.2 million input tokens and 1.8 million output, $32.40. My account is on the provider's free tier, its lowest price plan, which allows 12 calls a minute. It offers a spend limit, a monthly cap on the bill. I never set one.

comments.author: u/tower_six_halvard
comments.text: That was me, last Tuesday. I'm home now, at the bottom of the hill. The footsteps were the tower. On a cold night after a hot day the steel settles one landing at a time, from the ground up, slow, like someone climbing. There are fourteen landings. I counted them all night from the cab. It stops at the top. Tell Marisol to talk to it. I did.

replies.author: u/repeater_hut_teun
replies.text: I read her your comment on the radio at four. She was quiet for a while. Then she said the stairs had stopped, at fourteen.

comments.author: u/overnight_invoice_zuzana
comments.text: Station busy will be a 429. Every HTTP response starts with a status code, a three-digit number saying how the request went, and 429 means too many requests: the account went over its rate limit. Ours came with a retry-after header, a name: value line on the response saying how many seconds to wait. Our nightly report job ignored it and asked again at once, and every one of those retries was refused too. It took us a week to notice the limit wasn't per program: the report job and our support bot shared one account, so on the bad nights the bot went quiet as well.

replies.author: u/repeater_hut_teun
replies.text: Ours said retry-after: 5. My page asked again at once, five more times for each of the ten towers. Sixty refusals inside one second, and two calls through.

reply.prompt: The net opens at nine tonight, and the stranger's calls start at eleven. What should Teun change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Clear every tower's saved conversation and take the page's link off the noticeboard. The API key can stay where it is: if nobody new can find the page, nobody new can read the API key.
options.verdict: Hiding the page didn't hide the key
options.part2: I cleared every conversation and took the link down at noon. At 01:47 Marisol asked her question again, and the answer came back clean: 65 tokens in, 33 out, end_turn, no Halvard, no stairs. But the usage page had started again at eleven: ten calls at the top of every minute. At the 02:00 roll call ten of my twelve towers heard station busy, and my page asked again at once, five times for each: 60 refusals. Whoever had the key never needed the link again.
options.senior: A copied API key works until you revoke it, wherever the original lives. Clearing the history fixed one night's answer; deciding on purpose what each request carries fixes every night's.

options.text: Revoke the API key, paste a new one into the page with a monthly spend limit, and clear each tower's conversation at every shift change. It's an hour's work, and the limit caps any new leak.
options.verdict: Trade-off: tonight is fixed, the next leak is booked
options.part2: New key in the page by noon, with a $10 monthly spend limit, and the page now forgets each tower's conversation at the shift change. Marisol's question came back clean: 65 tokens in, 33 out, end_turn. The roll call went through, twelve of twelve. Four nights later the usage page showed ten calls at the top of every minute again: the new key sat on the same line of the same page. The limit held the stranger to $10. Then it held us too: from just before one, every tower's call came back refused, and the far station was silent until I raised it.
options.senior: Revoking first was right, and a spend limit is a good backstop. But any API key you send to a browser will be read again, and a limit a stranger can reach switches you off along with them. The key has to stop leaving your own machines.

options.text: Revoke the API key now. Put a small server between the page and the provider: it holds a new key and the standing orders, keeps each shift's conversation, caps calls, and waits before retrying.
options.part2: I revoked the key at noon, and the stranger's next calls came back 401, an authentication error. The old base laptop is now a small server in the cupboard. The page talks only to it. It adds the new API key, kept in a setting outside the code, the standing orders as the system prompt, and only this shift's turns for each tower, cleared at the handover. It caps each tower at six calls a minute, texts me if a night passes $1, and after a 429 waits 5 seconds, then 10, then 20. I raised max_tokens to 80, and any answer that still stops at max_tokens goes on air with the words answer cut. At 01:47 Marisol asked again: 65 tokens in, 33 out, end_turn. At the 02:00 roll call all twelve towers answered first time. At three I opened the usage page. Nothing on the hour.
options.senior: An API key belongs where only your own code can read it, and the request belongs to your server: it decides what history goes in and under which role, how long the answer may run, and how long to wait after a 429. Revoke first: a copied key works until you do.

options.text: Keep the page as it is, buy the provider's next tier so the roll call fits under the limit, and have the page retry every refused call at once until it gets through, so nobody hears busy.
options.verdict: Paying more to keep the stranger fed
options.part2: I bought the next tier, 60 calls a minute, and set the page to retry at once until it got through. At the 02:00 roll call all twelve towers answered first time. Everything else stayed. The stranger's ten calls at the top of every minute kept coming, $32.40 a night on my card. At 01:47 the far station called Marisol Halvard again and stopped at Stay in the. On Friday the provider was overloaded for twenty minutes, and my page asked again at once, over and over, every call refused, until the laptop's fan was the loudest thing in the base.
options.senior: A 429 asks you to slow down: its retry-after says how long, and earlier retries fail. Retrying at once only adds refusals, and a higher limit raises the ceiling for whoever holds your key too. Fix who can call before how often.

sim.title: Build the far station's request yourself
sim.lede: You're Teun at four in the morning with the page's saved 01:47 request open. This console never sends anything anywhere: it builds the HTTP request the page would send, shaped like Anthropic's Messages API, headers included, so you can set it beside the reference; shows the station's scripted answer, whose stop reason is end_turn when it finished on its own and max_tokens when it was cut; and works out the numbers. Token counts are teaching token counts, one per word, number or punctuation mark, so they differ from a real tokenizer's (case 3). The model name, teaching-station-1, is made up, and so are the teaching prices, the story provider's: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. You choose whether the system prompt goes in, how many of Halvard's four saved turns go back in before Marisol's question, max_tokens, and temperature, which can be left out. The API key's header is always shown as [hidden]. The station is a toy: it answers from whether the system prompt and Halvard's turns arrived. Where the API key lives sets who can read it: in the page's browser code, in a public repository (a folder of code anyone online can read), or in an environment variable (a setting the server's program reads when it starts) on the base server. The drill replays the 02:00 roll call against a teaching rate limit: the account holds 12 calls, refilled at one every 5 seconds, and a refused call gets a 429 with retry-after, the seconds to wait. The stranger's script takes ten calls at the top of every minute. Retries can be none, at once (five more tries, like Teun's page), or growing waits of 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 seconds.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start on the 01:47 request: system prompt on, 4 of Halvard's turns, max_tokens 40, temperature 0.3, the API key in the page's browser code. It's 255 tokens in, and the reply stops at Stay in the: stop_reason max_tokens, 40 tokens out, 0.000910 dollars. Slide the past turns down one at a time: 208, 167, 126, then 65 at zero, and Halvard leaves the answer, which now ends on its own: end_turn, 33 tokens. Put the turns back to 4 and raise max_tokens to 80: the whole 49-token answer arrives, stairs and all. Turn the system prompt off: 213 tokens in, and the reply loses its call sign and runs to 78 tokens. Move the API key to the server and read who can see it. In the drill you start on last night's roll call: the stranger on, 12 calls at once, retries at once: 2 served, 60 refusals, and 10 towers hear station busy. Pick growing waits: all 12 served by 02:01:15, after 29 refusals. Then switch the stranger off, which is what revoking the key does to him: 12 of 12, first time, no refusals.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at Kettlewood is haunted. The far station is a stateless model behind an API: it answered the conversation Teun's page sent, which was Halvard's, and stopped where max_tokens told it to. The stranger on his call sign is whoever read the API key out of his page, and was spending his account's limit and money.

steps.title: A call to a model is one HTTP request you build yourself.
steps.text: Teun's page did what every app that uses a hosted model does: it sent an HTTP request, a POST, to the provider's messages endpoint and waited for the response. Headers ride on top: the API key, which says which account is calling, a version header, and a content type saying the body is JSON. The body has a handful of fields. Anthropic's Messages API reference lists model, the model that will complete your prompt; max_tokens, the maximum number of tokens to generate before stopping; messages, the conversation; and system, the system prompt. Case 6's sampling settings, such as temperature, are optional fields, and they are changing: the same reference now marks temperature deprecated, saying models released after Claude Opus 4.6 do not support setting it, and a value other than 1.0 is rejected with a 400 error. The far station answered in about a second because nobody was far away: a model wrote about forty tokens and stopped.

steps.title: Messages and roles: the model continues whatever conversation you send.
steps.text: messages is a list, and each entry has a role and some content. Anthropic's reference says its models are trained to operate on alternating user and assistant conversational turns, and that consecutive turns with the same role are combined into one. Anthropic counts each message as a turn; this course keeps case 9's meaning, a message and its answer, so Halvard's four turns are eight messages. The system prompt sits outside the list: the reference calls it a way of providing context and instructions, such as specifying a particular goal or role. It is case 9's instructions, given a field of their own. Because the API is stateless, you always send the full conversational history, and the model can't check where that history came from: Anthropic's guide notes that earlier turns don't need to come from Claude at all. Teun's page saved each tower's conversation and never cleared it, so at 01:47 it sent Halvard's four turns, eight messages, then Marisol's question: 255 tokens in, 190 of them Halvard's. The model did what it was trained to do and continued the conversation it was given, which was Halvard's. The newest Claude models also accept a system message later in a conversation, but standing orders belong in the top-level system field.

steps.title: The response says what it wrote, why it stopped, and what it cost.
steps.text: A successful response carries content, a list of blocks whose text is the answer; stop_reason; and usage, the input and output tokens you are billed for, case 3's arithmetic. Anthropic's stop-reason guide lists end_turn when the model finished its response naturally, max_tokens when the response reached your max_tokens limit, stop_sequence when it emitted one of your stop sequences, and a few more: for tools, for when the model declines to answer, and for a full context window. The guide separates these from errors: a stop reason comes with a successful response, while a failed request comes back as an HTTP status code in the 4xx or 5xx range. max_tokens is a ceiling, not a target, and the reference says models may stop before reaching it. Teun's answer would have run to 49 tokens; his cap was 40, so the station stopped at Stay in the, and the page read it on air without looking at stop_reason. Anthropic's advice for a cut answer is to raise max_tokens or continue the response; at the least, say it was cut. At the teaching prices, $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, that call cost 910 millionths of a dollar.

steps.title: The API key is who pays, so it must never reach a browser.
steps.text: Anthropic's key guide puts it plainly: your API key is a digital key to your account, and much like a credit card number, if someone obtains and uses your API key, they incur charges on your behalf. Anything a browser loads can be read by whoever opens the page, which is why Anthropic's TypeScript SDK leaves web browsers disabled by default to avoid exposing your secret API credentials, unless you set an option named dangerouslyAllowBrowser. Teun's key sat in his page's code, and the page's link was public, so whoever found it got his account: his limits and his bill. A key pushed to a public GitHub repository is more likely to be caught: Anthropic says GitHub scans public repositories for exposed Claude API keys, and Anthropic then deactivates the key and emails its owner. Browser code gets no such check. The fix is in the design: browsers talk to your own server, the server holds the key and adds it to each request, and the key lives in an environment variable or, better, a secrets manager. If a key may have leaked, Anthropic recommends revoking it immediately, and rotating keys on a schedule, for example every 90 days.

steps.title: Errors: retry the ones that pass, fix the ones that don't.
steps.text: Anthropic's errors page lists the status codes and error types you will meet. 400 invalid_request_error: something is wrong with the format or content of your request, such as a temperature the model no longer accepts; retrying won't help. 401 authentication_error: a problem with your API key, for example malformed, revoked or expired; it's what a stranger gets once the key is revoked. 429 rate_limit_error: your organization has hit a rate limit. 500 api_error: something unexpected broke inside the provider, and the page says to retry with exponential backoff. 529 overloaded_error: the API is temporarily overloaded, which can happen under high traffic across all users. The rate-limit page explains the 429: limits use the token bucket algorithm, so capacity refills continuously; a rate of 60 requests per minute might be enforced as 1 request per second, so short bursts can trip it; and the 429 carries a retry-after header, the number of seconds to wait, before which retries will fail. So for 429, 500 and 529, wait at least that long when a retry-after is given, then longer each time with a little jitter, and give up after a few tries. Anthropic's SDK does this for you, twice by default. Two catches. A 429 for a used-up monthly spend cap has no retry-after and keeps failing. A spend limit you set yourself, below that cap, comes back as a 400 invalid_request_error instead, and retrying won't help either. And limits are set at the organization level, not per key, so anyone holding your key spends your limit, as the stranger's ten calls did at 02:00. Season 6 covers retries, timeouts and fallbacks in production.

diagram.aria: The far station after the fix. Top row: the wardens' page, in the browser with no API key, sends the question to the base server, which holds the API key and adds the system prompt, and sends the request to the provider, a stateless model behind POST /v1/messages. Bottom row: the conversations, one per tower per shift, cleared at handover, feed their turns to the server; limits and alerts, calls per tower, a spend alert and backoff, decide whether a call may go; the response, with content and stop_reason, and usage counting tokens in and out, comes back and its usage is counted against the limits. A note says the API key never leaves the server.

notes.text: the API key never leaves the server

explain.caption: Read left to right along the top. The wardens' page sends only the question, with no API key in it. The base server builds the request: the key from outside its code, the standing orders as the system prompt, and this shift's turns for that tower as messages, if the limits allow the call. The provider's stateless model answers. The response's stop_reason is checked before anything goes on air, and its usage is counted against the spend alert.

fix.title: The fix: revoke the key, then put a small server between the page and the provider
fix.text: Revoke the leaked API key first, because every copy works until you do; a new key is a minute's work. Then stop sending the key to browsers at all. A small server at the base receives each question from the wardens' page, which needs its own sign-in, and builds the request itself: the new key from an environment variable for now, or a secrets manager as the net grows; the standing orders as the system prompt; and the turns of this tower's current shift as messages, cleared at the handover, so nobody is ever answered as last week's warden. Size max_tokens for the longest good answer, check stop_reason on every response, and say on air when an answer was cut. Put limits where a stranger can't reach them: calls per tower, a spend alert that fires within the hour, and a spend limit as a backstop. On a 429, 500 or 529, wait at least retry-after when the response carries one, then longer each time, and give up after a few tries with a clear message instead of a storm of retries. With the stranger gone, the sim's roll call goes through twelve of twelve, first time, and Marisol's question costs 65 tokens in and 33 out.

limits: The server is now the thing to guard. Anyone who can reach it can spend through it, so it needs a sign-in for the wardens, its own limits and a log of calls. An environment variable keeps the API key out of the code, but OWASP warns that environment variables are generally accessible to all processes and may be included in logs or system dumps; a secrets manager, with every read logged, is the stronger home.

Fresh conversations and a bigger max_tokens are choices, not cures. Clearing each shift loses context a warden might need, so decide what carries over, such as a short handover note; case 4 of this season is about choosing what goes in. A higher cap prevents most cut-offs, not all, so stop_reason is checked on every response.

Backoff helps with bursts and a busy provider, not with a stolen API key or a used-up spend cap, whose 429 has no retry-after. Standards readiness: if your organisation is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001 certification, API keys are authentication information under Annex A control 5.17, which expects a managed process for issuing and handling them; if it is pursuing a SOC 2 report, the logical access criteria (the CC6 series) cover how access is granted, protected and removed. Build key storage, rotation and access logs in from the first version, not at audit time.

explain.seniorTake: An LLM API call is an HTTP request you assemble. The model sees exactly the messages you send, in the roles you give them, plus the system prompt, and nothing else, and it bills whoever's API key is on the header. So own the request on a server: keep the key there, decide what history goes in, size max_tokens and read stop_reason, and treat 429s and overloads as weather to wait out, not a wall to hammer through.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: the Messages API keeps no conversation
realWorld.text: Anthropic's guide to the Messages API says: the Messages API is stateless, which means that you always send the full conversational history to the API. Earlier conversational turns don't necessarily need to actually originate from Claude; you can use synthetic assistant messages. Its sample response shows what comes back: an id, the role assistant, a content list holding a text block, the model, a stop_reason of end_turn, a stop_sequence of null (empty, because no stop sequence fired), and usage with input_tokens and output_tokens. Its example request sends three headers: x-api-key, anthropic-version set to 2023-06-01, and content-type set to application/json.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: the request fields
realWorld.text: The Messages API reference says the models are trained to operate on alternating user and assistant conversational turns, that you specify the prior turns with the messages parameter and the model generates the next message, and that consecutive user or assistant turns in your request will be combined into a single turn. max_tokens is the maximum number of tokens to generate before stopping, and the models may stop before reaching it. The system prompt is a way of providing context and instructions to Claude, such as specifying a particular goal or role. temperature is marked deprecated: models released after Claude Opus 4.6 do not support setting temperature, a value of 1.0 will be accepted for backwards compatibility, and all other values will be rejected. The guide adds that temperature, top_p and top_k are not supported on Claude 4.7 and later models, and setting them to a non-default value returns a 400 error.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: why a response stopped
realWorld.text: Anthropic's guide to stop reasons says every Messages API response includes a stop_reason field that tells you why Claude stopped generating. Its list starts with end_turn, Claude finished its response naturally; max_tokens, the response reached your max_tokens limit; and stop_sequence, Claude emitted one of your stop_sequences. The rest cover tools (tool_use, Claude is calling a tool, and pause_turn), refusal, Claude declined to respond, and model_context_window_exceeded, the response filled the model's context window. For a max_tokens stop it advises: raise max_tokens or continue the response. It separates stop reasons, part of a successful response with valid content, from errors, HTTP status codes 4xx or 5xx that indicate request processing failures.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: the errors you will meet
realWorld.text: Anthropic's errors page lists 400 invalid_request_error, an issue with the format or content of your request; 401 authentication_error, an issue with your API key, for example malformed, revoked or expired; 429 rate_limit_error, your organization has hit a rate limit; 500 api_error, an unexpected error internal to Anthropic's systems, to be retried with exponential backoff; and 529 overloaded_error, the API is temporarily overloaded, which can occur when the API experiences high traffic across all users. It notes that the official SDK automatically retries transient failures, such as connection errors, rate limits and 5xx server errors, with exponential backoff, twice by default, honoring the retry-after header when present. Every response also carries a request-id header to quote to support.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: rate limits
realWorld.text: Anthropic's rate-limit page says limits are set at the organization level, and that the API uses the token bucket algorithm, so your capacity is continuously replenished up to your maximum limit, rather than being reset at fixed intervals. You might hit limits over shorter time intervals: a rate of 60 requests per minute might be enforced as 1 request per second, and short bursts of requests can exceed the limit and trigger rate limit errors. A 429 describes which limit was exceeded and carries a retry-after header, the number of seconds to wait until you can retry the request, and earlier retries will fail. Once a tier's monthly spend cap is reached, requests return a 429 with no retry-after header, and retrying fails until access resumes.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: keeping API keys safe
realWorld.text: Anthropic's support guide to API key best practices says your API key is a digital key to your account, and much like a credit card number, if someone obtains and uses your API key, they incur charges on your behalf. It recommends environment variables, encrypted secret storage in cloud environments, separate keys for development, testing and production, rotating keys on a consistent schedule, for example every 90 days, and revoking a key immediately if you suspect it may be compromised. GitHub actively scans public repositories for exposed Claude API keys; when one is found, GitHub notifies Anthropic, Anthropic automatically deactivates the key, and the owner gets an email about it.

realWorld.title: Anthropic's SDK: browsers off by default
realWorld.text: The requirements of Anthropic's TypeScript SDK list web browsers as disabled by default to avoid exposing your secret API credentials, with browser support enabled by explicitly setting dangerouslyAllowBrowser to true. Its note on browser use explains that any user with access to the browser can potentially inspect, extract and misuse these credentials, and names the exceptions: internal tools used by trusted people, and development or debugging with short-lived keys that aren't used in production. The same SDK retries connection errors, rate limits and server errors 2 times by default, with a short exponential backoff.

realWorld.title: OWASP: secrets management
realWorld.text: OWASP's Secrets Management Cheat Sheet counts API keys among the secrets an organisation has to manage. It says you should regularly rotate secrets so that any stolen credentials will only work for a short time, and that when secrets are no longer required or potentially compromised, you must securely revoke them. On environment variables it is cautious: they are generally accessible to all processes and may be included in logs or system dumps, and it does not recommend them unless the other methods are not possible.

realWorld.title: Standards: ISO/IEC 27001
realWorld.text: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 is the international standard for an information security management system. Its Annex A control 5.17, authentication information, covers how secrets that prove identity are allocated and managed, including telling people how to handle them. It doesn't name API keys for language models, but an API key is exactly that kind of secret, so the control applies if your organisation is certified or heading that way.

realWorld.title: Standards: SOC 2
realWorld.text: A SOC 2 report is judged against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. Their logical access criteria, the CC6 series, cover how access to systems and data is granted, protected and removed. An auditor looking at an AI feature will ask the same questions this case does: where the API keys live, who can read them, and how a leaked one is revoked.

asked: Walk me through an LLM API call.
How do you keep conversation state?
Where should the API key live?
What happens when you hit a rate limit?
interview.answer: An LLM API call is one HTTP request. I POST JSON to the provider's messages endpoint with the API key in a header. The body names the model, sets max_tokens, the most it may write, carries a system prompt with the standing instructions, and a list of messages, each with a role, user or assistant, alternating and ending with the user's new message. Sampling settings such as temperature are optional, and some newer models reject them, so I check the reference for the model I use. The response has the content, a stop_reason, end_turn if it finished, max_tokens if it was cut off, stop_sequence if it hit one of mine, and usage, the input and output tokens I'm billed for. I check stop_reason before using the text, and I log usage per feature. Conversation state lives in my application, not the model: the API is stateless, so every call sends the history I choose, stored per conversation on my server, trimmed or summarized on purpose as it grows, with must-keep facts pinned, and never another user's turns. The API key proves which account pays, so it lives only on the server, in a secrets manager or at least an environment variable, never in browser code, a mobile app or a repository. Clients call my backend, which signs users in, applies per-user limits and adds the key. Keys are rotated on a schedule, a leaked one is revoked at once, and there's a spend alert. On a rate limit I get a 429 with a retry-after header. I wait at least that long, then retry with exponential backoff and jitter, cap the retries and fail with a clear message; retrying at once only adds refusals. 500s and 529 overloaded get the same treatment; 400s and 401s don't, because retrying an invalid request or a bad key never works. Limits are set per organization, so I spread bursts out, and if normal traffic hits them I ask for a higher tier.

terms.def: The wardens' name for Teun's relay page and the model behind it. Nothing far about it: a language model reached through a provider's API.
Teun's web page that turns a warden's question into a request to the model and reads the answer on air. It held the API key, the standing orders and every tower's saved conversation.
A tall tower on a ridge where a warden watches the forest for smoke and lightning strikes.
Here, the person on watch in a fire tower overnight.
The glass room at the top of a fire tower, where the warden sits.
The direction of something, given as an angle measured from north.
The name a radio station answers to on the air. Teun's way of saying his account: someone else is calling as him.
A check-in where every station on a radio net reports. At 02:00 Teun's page sends one call for each tower at once.
The change of shift, when one warden passes the tower to the next.
Hypertext Transfer Protocol: the web's way for one program to ask another for something. A client sends a request, and a server sends back a response.
The HTTP method for handing something over to be processed. A call to a model's messages endpoint is a POST.
An extra line on an HTTP request or response, written as name: value, such as retry-after: 5.
A three-digit number at the top of every HTTP response saying how the request went, such as 200 for success or 429 for too many requests.
JavaScript Object Notation: plain text made of labels and values, like {"max_tokens": 40}. Model APIs send and receive it.
A header saying what format a request's body is in. Calls to a model's API say application/json.
A header naming which version of an API a request expects. Anthropic's is anthropic-version, and its examples send 2023-06-01.
A secret string that proves which account is calling an API, so the provider knows whose limits to count and whose bill to charge. Not case 5's attention key.
Something that proves who you are to a system, such as a password or an API key.
Standing instructions sent with every request in a field of their own, outside the conversation: case 9's instructions. Teun's standing orders were 42 teaching tokens.
Teun's name for the far station's system prompt: answer in plain radio English, under 50 words, call sign first, end with Over.
One entry in a request's conversation: a role and some content. Halvard's four turns were eight messages.
The label on each message saying who wrote it: user for whoever asks, assistant for the model. The newest Claude models also accept a system message later in a conversation.
The most tokens the model may write in its answer. A ceiling, not a target: the answer stops there, finished or not, and the stop reason says max_tokens.
The stop_reason field in every successful response, saying why the model stopped writing: end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence and a few others.
The stop reason for an answer the model finished on its own.
A string you list in the request. If the model writes it, generation stops there and the stop reason is stop_sequence.
In a response, the part holding what the model wrote, as a list of blocks. A text block carries the answer.
In a response, the count of that call's input and output tokens, which is what you are billed for (case 3).
A Claude model. Anthropic's reference says models released after it do not support setting temperature.
A provider's page listing the calls made on an account, with their tokens and costs.
A provider's website for managing an account: API keys, limits, usage and billing.
To switch an API key off for good. Every copy stops working at once, and you make a new key for your own code.
To replace an API key with a new one on a schedule and revoke the old one, so a stolen key only works for a short time.
A provider's price plan for an account, which sets its rate limits and spend cap. Teun's free tier allows 12 calls a minute.
A monthly cap on an account's bill, set by you or by its tier. Once it is reached, the provider refuses calls until the month resets or the limit is raised.
A message the provider or your own code sends when spending passes a set amount, so a leak shows up in hours, not at the end of the month.
The status code for too many requests: the account went over a rate limit. Anthropic's error type for it is rate_limit_error.
A header on a 429 giving the number of seconds to wait before retrying. Anthropic's docs say earlier retries will fail.
The status code for a failed sign-in. Anthropic's authentication_error: the API key is malformed, revoked or expired.
The status code for an unexpected error inside the provider. Anthropic's api_error, worth retrying with backoff.
Anthropic's status code for overloaded_error: the API is temporarily overloaded, for example under high traffic across all users.
The name in an error response's body, such as invalid_request_error or rate_limit_error, saying what went wrong.
Sending a failed request again. Worth it for transient errors, useless for a malformed request or a revoked API key.
A failure that may pass on its own, such as a rate limit or an overloaded provider. The opposite of a mistake in your request.
Waiting longer after each failed try, for example 5, 10, then 20 seconds, so a struggling server or a spent limit gets room to recover.
A little randomness added to retry waits, so many clients don't all retry at the same instant.
A way to enforce a rate limit: the account holds a number of calls that refills steadily, so a burst can use what's saved, but no more.
Many requests sent at once, like Teun's roll call: twelve calls in the same second.
Anthropic's name for the account that owns API keys, limits and the bill. Its rate limits are set at this level, not for each key.
A named setting a program reads from the machine it runs on when it starts, so a secret can stay out of the code.
A service that stores secrets such as API keys encrypted, hands them only to programs allowed to read them, and logs every read.
The part of an app that runs on your own servers, out of users' reach. It can hold secrets that browsers and phones must never see.
A program that sits in front of another and passes requests through. Here, a small server that adds the API key to each call so browsers never see it.
The part of an app that runs on the user's machine, in a browser or a phone. Anyone using it can read its code.
A folder of code with its full history. A public one can be read by anyone online.
A popular website for hosting code repositories.
Software development kit: a provider's library that builds requests, retries errors and reads responses for you.
The programming language web pages run in the browser. Whoever loads the page can read it.
A programming language built on JavaScript, used for web pages and servers. Anthropic publishes an SDK for it.
A function your app lets the model ask to run, such as a search. Case 5 of this season covers tool calling.
Another sampling setting: draw the next token only from the k most likely. Like top_p, optional, and not accepted by Claude 4.7 and later models.
The Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a nonprofit that publishes free guides to building secure software.
ISO/IEC 27001's term for secrets that prove identity, such as passwords and keys. Annex A control 5.17 covers how they are issued and handled.
An auditor's report on a service company's security controls, judged against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. Many customers ask their suppliers for one.
The AICPA's criteria for SOC 2 reports. The logical access criteria, the CC6 series, cover how access to systems is granted, protected and removed.
The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants, which publishes the criteria SOC 2 reports use.
This case's made-up count: one token per word, number or punctuation mark. Real tokenizers count differently (case 3).
The sim's made-up model name. Real model names come from the provider's documentation.
The sim's made-up limit, the story's free tier: the account holds 12 calls, refilled at one every 5 seconds, 12 a minute.

atWork: Find every place at work that calls a model provider: services, scripts, notebooks, front ends and mobile apps. For each one, find where its API key lives, who can read it, and whether the same key is shared across development and production. Search your repositories, history included, for key-shaped strings. Then read the code around each call: does it check stop_reason before using the text, does it log usage, and what does it do on a 429, a 500 or a 529? Retries at once, retries forever and no retries are all common. A familiar story: a prototype calls the provider straight from the front end, someone reads the key out of the page, and the bill climbs overnight; the fix is a small backend proxy that holds the key, per-user limits, and a spend alert. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001 certification, API keys fall under Annex A control 5.17 on authentication information, and if it is pursuing a SOC 2 report, under the logical access criteria. Putting keys in a secrets manager with rotation and access logs now is far cheaper than retrofitting it before an audit.

recall.prompt: Your team's prototype chat page calls a model provider straight from the browser, with the API key in its JavaScript. This morning the bill had jumped, and the usage page shows thousands of overnight calls nobody on the team made. What do you do first, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Revoke the leaked key at once and issue a new one, because every copy works until it is switched off
Move the key off the client into a small backend that adds it to each request, kept in an environment variable or a secrets manager
Put limits where a stranger can't reach them: per-user limits, a spend alert or limit, and a regular look at what each key spends

recall.model: First I'd revoke the key in the provider's console and make a new one, because whoever copied it can keep calling until it is switched off; then I'd check what the copied key did. I wouldn't put the new key back in the page: anything a browser loads can be read. Instead a small backend proxy takes the page's requests, checks who is signed in, and adds the key from an environment variable or, better, a secrets manager, so the key never leaves our servers. I'd add per-user limits on that backend, a spend alert that fires within hours and a spend limit as a backstop, and I'd monitor usage per key so a leak shows up the same night. Finally I'd search our repositories for any other keys in code.

recall.prompt: Why did the far station call Marisol by Halvard's name?
options: The model remembered Halvard from last week and mixed up the two wardens
The provider's servers sent her an answer meant for someone else's call
The page sent Halvard's saved turns with her question, as one conversation
The system prompt told the station to greet each tower's usual warden
recall.why: The model keeps nothing between requests (case 9). Teun's page saved Tower 6's conversation and sent Halvard's four turns, eight messages, before her question: 255 tokens in, 190 of them Halvard's. The model continued the conversation it was given. The system prompt said nothing about names.

recall.prompt: A new teammate asks what actually goes over the wire when your app calls a language model, and what comes back. Explain in plain words.

keyIdeas.idea: One HTTP request to the provider's endpoint, with the API key in a header
A JSON body: the model name, max_tokens, a system prompt, and messages labelled with user and assistant roles
The whole conversation goes every time, because the model is stateless
Back come the text, a stop reason and the token counts you are billed for

recall.model: It's one HTTP request: a POST to the provider's messages endpoint, with our API key in a header so they know which account pays. The body is JSON: which model, max_tokens, the most it may write, a system prompt with our standing instructions, and the messages, each labelled with a role, user for the person and assistant for the model's earlier answers, ending with the newest user message. The model is stateless, so the whole conversation we want it to see goes every time. What comes back is the answer's text, a stop reason, end_turn if it finished or max_tokens if it was cut off, and usage: the input and output tokens we're billed for.

recall.prompt: An answer comes back with stop_reason max_tokens. What does that tell you?
options: The request failed, and the provider will send the rest in a second response
The answer hit your max_tokens cap and was cut off, so it may be unfinished
The model ran out of things to say before it reached your cap on output
Your account went over its rate limit, so the answer was shortened to fit
recall.why: A stop reason is part of a successful response, not an error. max_tokens means the model reached your cap and stopped, like the far station at Stay in the: 40 tokens of a 49-token answer. Finishing on its own gives end_turn. A rate limit comes back as a 429 error, with no answer at all.

recall.prompt: At the roll call, ten calls come back 429 with retry-after: 5. What should the client do?
options: Retry each call at once, as many times as it takes, so nobody has to wait
Treat 429 as a broken request and drop the calls without trying again
Send the refused calls with a second API key from the same account instead
Wait at least the 5 seconds, then retry with longer waits, and give up after a few
recall.why: A 429 means slow down. Anthropic's rate-limit page says retry-after is the number of seconds to wait until you can retry, and earlier retries will fail. In the sim's drill, retrying at once five times turns 10 refusals into 60 and serves nobody extra; waiting 5, then 10, 20 and 40 seconds serves all twelve by 02:01:15. A second key from the same account shares its limits, which Anthropic sets at the organization level.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The far station has run through the base server all season, and the stranger never came back. Now the forestry office wants it in a phone app for the wardens. Their contractor, Ottar, plans to build the API key into the app, since it's compiled and nobody can read it, send only the newest question to save tokens, and retry any failed call every half second until it goes through.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What would you tell Ottar, and how would you build it?

keyIdeas.idea: An app's code can be unpacked and read: keep the API key off the phone and send calls through your own backend, with sign-in and per-user limits
The model is stateless: a follow-up needs the earlier turns sent again with their roles, trimmed or summarized on purpose rather than dropped
Retry only transient errors such as 429, 500 and 529, waiting at least retry-after and longer each time, then give up
Watch spending and be ready to revoke: a spend alert, a spend limit and a log of calls

coldCase.model: Tell Ottar the API key can't go in the app. A compiled app can be unpacked and its strings extracted, and whoever pulls the key out gets our account, which is how the stranger got it last time. The app should talk only to our own backend: wardens sign in, the server adds the key from a secrets manager, applies per-user limits and logs every call. Sending only the newest question breaks follow-ups, because the model is stateless: it only knows the earlier turns if we send them again with their roles, so the server keeps each shift's conversation and trims or summarizes it on purpose. Retrying every half second turns one 429 into a storm: retry only transient errors such as 429, 500 and 529, wait at least the retry-after, then longer each time with jitter, and give up after a few tries with a clear message. And keep the spend alert and a spend limit, so a mistake shows up within hours, with the key ready to revoke in a minute.

sources.title: Anthropic, Using the Messages API (Claude Platform docs), as checked in October 2026: the Messages API is stateless, which means that you always send the full conversational history to the API; earlier conversational turns don't necessarily need to actually originate from Claude, synthetic assistant messages; example request with x-api-key, anthropic-version 2023-06-01 and content-type application/json headers, model, max_tokens and messages; example responses with id, type, role, content, model, stop_reason end_turn or max_tokens, stop_sequence null and usage input_tokens and output_tokens; temperature, top_p and top_k not supported on Claude 4.7 and later models, a non-default value returns a 400 error; system role messages after a user turn on the newest models, the top-level system field for instructions that apply from the start

Anthropic, Messages API reference, Create a Message (Claude Platform docs), as checked in October 2026: POST /v1/messages with x-api-key and anthropic-version headers; models are trained to operate on alternating user and assistant conversational turns; consecutive user or assistant turns are combined into a single turn; max_tokens, the maximum number of tokens to generate before stopping, and models may stop before reaching it; system prompt, a way of providing context and instructions to Claude, such as specifying a particular goal or role; temperature deprecated: models released after Claude Opus 4.6 do not support setting temperature, a value of 1.0 is accepted for backwards compatibility and all other values are rejected; stop_sequences and the stop_sequence response field

Anthropic, Handling stop reasons (Claude Platform docs), as checked in October 2026: every Messages API response includes a stop_reason field; end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, tool_use, pause_turn, refusal, model_context_window_exceeded; for max_tokens, raise max_tokens or continue the response; stop reasons are part of successful responses, errors are HTTP status codes 4xx or 5xx

Anthropic, Claude API errors (Claude Platform docs), as checked in October 2026: 400 invalid_request_error, 401 authentication_error (malformed, revoked or expired API key), 429 rate_limit_error, 500 api_error (retry with exponential backoff), 529 overloaded_error (high traffic across all users); the official SDK retries transient failures with exponential backoff, twice by default, honoring the retry-after header; request-id header on every response

Anthropic, Rate limits (Claude Platform docs), as checked in October 2026: limits are set at the organization level; token bucket algorithm, capacity continuously replenished up to your maximum limit; 60 requests per minute might be enforced as 1 request per second, short bursts can exceed the limit; a 429 with a retry-after header, the number of seconds to wait until you can retry, earlier retries will fail; a tier's monthly spend cap returns 429 with no retry-after header; a spend limit you set returns 400

Anthropic Help Center, API Key Best Practices: Keeping Your Keys Safe and Secure (updated March 2026, checked October 2026): your API key is a digital key to your account; much like a credit card number, if someone obtains and uses your API key, they incur charges on your behalf; environment variables; encrypted secret storage in cloud environments; separate keys per environment; rotate on a consistent schedule, for example every 90 days; revoke immediately if compromised; GitHub scans public repositories for exposed Claude API keys, notifies Anthropic, Anthropic deactivates the key and emails the owner

Anthropic, TypeScript SDK (Claude Platform docs), as checked in October 2026: web browsers disabled by default to avoid exposing your secret API credentials, enabled by explicitly setting dangerouslyAllowBrowser to true; any user with access to the browser can potentially inspect, extract and misuse these credentials; exceptions for internal tools and short-lived development credentials; connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and 500 and above retried 2 times by default with a short exponential backoff

OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, Secrets Management Cheat Sheet: API keys among the secrets to manage; regularly rotate secrets so that any stolen credentials will only work for a short time (2.7.2); revoke secrets that are no longer required or potentially compromised (2.7.3); environment variables are generally accessible to all processes and may be included in logs or system dumps, not recommended unless the other methods are not possible (5.1)

ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection, Information security management systems, Requirements: Annex A control 5.17, authentication information (allocation and management of authentication information controlled by a management process, including advice to personnel on handling it)
AICPA, 2017 Trust Services Criteria (With Revised Points of Focus, 2022): the criteria used for SOC 2 reports, including the common criteria for logical and physical access controls (CC6 series)
